chapter: Le Ruban Bleu, retirement and community work
title: 'My Old Friends': from La MaMa to Broadway
summary: She got involved through Phil Rose; the show opened Off-Off-Broadway in 1978 and moved to a midtown theater, running April to May.

story.theme_name: Radio and television work: staff jobs, shows and broadcasts
story.community_name: Working radio and television: network shows, studio staffs, talk-show bands

blocks.x: Yeah. Well, I guess through the fact that I was doing "My Old Friends" two years ago. I got involved in this stage production. I got a call from some woman. Her name was Rosetta Reitz, I found out. She said there's a show going into rehearsal and there's a part in it for you. So she said if you're interested to call Phil Rose who was the Director.

So I got in touch with Phil Rose who she mentioned as the Director. And I called Phil and I said, "I hear you have a play," you know, "where there's a part in it that might be for me, you know, a senior citizen." And I think he was a little surprised to hear from me because he hadn't seen me in a long time or heard from me. So he said, well it isn't very much of a part. So I said, well I'd like to read the script

anyway. So I went down and in the meantime he had got in touch with Norman Sacks and Mel Mandel who had written the music. Mel wrote the book and Norman Sacks wrote the music. So neither one of them knew anything about Maxine Sullivan and they were too young to know. So anyway, Mel said he went out and bought the book The Street That Never Slept. And of course when Arnold Shaw was putting the book together he came up here to the house and interviewed me. In the book are alot of quotes in there, you know, things that I mentioned. And I was talking to him about the time I went down to Blue's Alley and I sang down there, and at the end I said, you know, there's still a little spark left in the old girl yet. So they went out and wrote a song, "There's Still A Little Spark Left In The Old Girl Yet". And I got a Tony Nomination for my performance in the show.
Okay now, "MY Old Friends" was Off- and then Off-Broadway on Off-Broadway at first/and then finally On Broadway at the 22 Steps Theater.
Yeah, well we actually opened at La MaMa, Off-Off-Broadway as experimental.
That was at the end of 1978?
S. & S. REPORTING COMPANY, INC. WOrth 2-2915 WOrth 2-2943

Yeah, 1978. And Mel Mandel who wrote the book and it was written for seniors, you know, about seniors, and Andrew Stein who is the Borough President of Manhattan became interested because one of his projects has to do with senior citizens. He's very interested. So it seems that he put up the money for the show to open at the La Mama. And part of the arrangement was that we would do "My Old Friends" in each of the five boroughs. That we would do a performance in each of the five boroughs. So we did and of course the show got very good notices. And we did performances in Long Island, Queens Community College, and we played twice at the 92nd Street Y. We played in Brooklyn. I forget what the theater was there. And at Co-op City here in the Bronx. And as I said before, it got very good notices and it was received beautifully. And then they finally got some backers and produced at the Orpheum Theater. We moved out of the Off-Broadway theater because you can only do so many Off-Broadway performances anyway. So we moved into the Orpheum in January of '79. And we stayed there until around April of '79. In the meantime the producer was looking around for a theater

at mid-town in Manhattan. So a theater had opened in mid-town on the sight of the old Latin Quarter which years ago was the Cotton Club, the site of the old Cotton Club. And so we moved into the, they call it the 22 Steps Theatre. So we moved in there and we had a short engagement there because, I don't know what happened, what happened was when you move into a theatre part of the arrangement was that if you don't gross a certain amount of money in a week. Then the manager had the option to lease the theater to another company. I understand that this option isn't always exercised, but in this particular case there was a show, Phyllis Newman had her one woman show and she wanted the theatre. And she came in with "The Mad Woman Of Central Park West". And we had to get out and we couldn't find another theatre small enough because the production was small. We felt that a theatre holding more than five hundred people wouldn't approve. We had a theatre of twenty-five hundred people and we couldn't - I would think had we been up there a little longer we would have gotten the audience. I know alot of people who missed it, who kept putting it off and wanted to see it, thought it was going to be there for-

ever because of the notices but not knowing what goes on on Broadway they just waited too long. And then with the other production coming in we had to get out of there.
Yes. I forget how many performances we did there. We closed in May but altogether in the three theaters we did 155 performances.
